concept.name: Core inflation
concept.definition: An inflation measure that excludes the volatile food and energy components, intended to reveal the underlying, persistent trend in prices. In the U.S. the standard readings are 'all items less food and energy' in the CPI and the core PCE price index.
concept.intuition: Gasoline and grocery prices whipsaw month to month; stripping them out gives a cleaner read on whether inflation is really embedded in the economy, which is what central banks care about.
concept.mechanics: Statistical agencies compute the same price index over the basket minus food and energy items and report its monthly and 12-month changes alongside headline figures. The concept of excluding food and energy originated in the 1970s when oil shocks made headline inflation noisy; the Fed's 2% target is defined on PCE, with core PCE watched as the trend gauge.
concept.formula: Core inflation rate = (CoreIndex_t / CoreIndex_{t-12} - 1) x 100, where the core index is the CPI (or PCE index) excluding food and energy components.
concept.failure_modes: Food and energy shocks can persist and pass through into core (second-round effects), so core can understate true inflation pressure for long stretches; shelter measurement lags also distort core readings.
concept.misconceptions: Core inflation is not a claim that food and energy 'don't matter' to households — it is a signal-extraction device for policy, not a measure of the cost of living.
concept.example: In June 2026, headline CPI rose 3.5% over 12 months while the index for all items less food and energy rose 2.6%, showing energy drove much of the headline overshoot.
